crash","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Why careful drivers need this.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-F05"]},{"text":"Stopping, exchanging, calling.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"This chapter covers what to do after a traffic crash. The manual begins by noting that more than three hundred thousand crashes happen in the state each year, and that they strike even careful, lawful drivers through surprises and other people's mistakes. So every driver needs to know what to do at the scene and what the reporting law requires. In this first lesson we cover the duty to stop, the two kinds of leaving the scene, the information drivers must exchange, what to do when you damage unattended property, and calling for help when someone is hurt.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Be ready, then stop","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Crashes reach careful drivers too.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]},{"text":"Carry flares and a first-aid kit.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]},{"text":"Every crash demands a stop.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Because crashes strike even careful drivers, the manual suggests keeping flares and a first-aid kit in the car, which you can buy at department or auto stores. When a crash happens, the first duty is simple: stop. Every crash demands a stop, whatever the damage. Leaving a scene where there is only property damage counts as a traffic violation. Leaving a scene where someone was injured or killed counts as a crime. So no crash is too small to stop for, and the more serious the crash, the more serious the offense of driving away from it.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Exchange the details","fact_ids":["sec12-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Name, address, license, registration.","fact_ids":["sec12-F03"]},{"text":"Insurance with policy number and date.","fact_ids":["sec12-F03"]},{"text":"Show insurance cards on demand.","fact_ids":["sec12-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Even when a crash causes only property damage, you must exchange information with the other drivers involved and with any police at the scene. That means your name, address, license, registration, and insurance, including the policy number and the effective date. You also show your insurance card when asked. So keep your license, registration and insurance card where you can reach them. The exchange is required for every crash with another driver, not just the serious ones, and the insurance details include more than the company name.","fact_ids":["sec12-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Unattended property and injuries","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Parked car, property or animal hit?","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},{"text":"Find the owner or call police.","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},{"text":"Injury or death: call police at once.","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"If you damage a parked vehicle, other property that is not a vehicle, or a domestic animal, you must find the owner or notify the police. Driving away without doing either is not an option. If anyone is injured or killed, call the police at once, and confirm that an ambulance or rescue is on the way. So the duties grow with the harm. Property damage means exchanging details or finding the owner. Any injury or death means calling the police immediately and making sure medical help is coming before anything else is done at the scene.","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two kinds of flight","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Property-only scene: traffic violation.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02"]},{"text":"Injury or fatal scene: criminal.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02"]},{"text":"Stop every time.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Some drivers think leaving a minor crash is no big deal, or that leaving any crash is treated the same way. The manual describes one duty to stop with two kinds of flight. Fleeing a property-only scene breaks traffic law. Fleeing an injury or fatal scene breaks criminal law. So the stop itself is never optional, but the consequence of leaving depends on whether anyone was hurt. The safe and legal choice is the same in every case: stop, exchange the required information, and call for help if anyone is injured.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the flight rule","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02","sec12-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Leaving an injury crash.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02","sec12-F05"]},{"text":"What kind of offense?","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02","sec12-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a driver leaves the scene of a crash in which someone was injured. What kind of offense is that? Work it out before reading on. The answer is a crime. Leaving a scene with only property damage is a traffic violation, but leaving an injury or fatal scene counts as criminal. In either case the duty was the same: every crash demands a stop. And with an injury, the driver should have called the police at once and confirmed that an ambulance or rescue was on the way. One stop, two kinds of flight, and the stop comes first every time.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F02","sec12-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"At the scene in short","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-R01","sec12-F03","sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop after every crash.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-R01","sec12-F03","sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},{"text":"Exchange the full details.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-R01","sec12-F03","sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},{"text":"Call police at once for injuries.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-R01","sec12-F03","sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, crashes strike even careful drivers, so carry flares and a first-aid kit and know your duties. Every crash demands a stop. Leaving a property-only scene is a traffic violation, and leaving an injury or fatal scene is criminal. Exchange name, address, license, registration and insurance, including the policy number and effective date, with other drivers and police. If you harm a parked vehicle, other property or a domestic animal, find the owner or notify police. Any injury or death means calling police at once. Next we look at keeping the scene wires.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F08","sec12-F09"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"When may you move an injured person at a crash scene?","fact_ids":["sec12-F08"]},"answer":{"text":"Only when safe","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Clearing and guarding the scene.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-F09"]},{"text":"The injured and downed wires.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers keeping a crash scene safe. The manual explains what to do with the vehicles and how to warn other traffic, what drivers who were not involved should do, when an injured person may be moved and how, and what to do about downed power wires. Several of these rules ask you to hold back rather than act, which can feel unnatural in an emergency. So we will look closely at when to move an injured person and when to stay put, and at why both rescuers and occupants wait when wires are down. Each of these rules protects the people at the scene, including you.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Clear and guard","fact_ids":["sec12-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Move vehicles off the road if able.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06"]},{"text":"Use reflectors or flares.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06"]},{"text":"Guard against fuel and traffic.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"If you can, move the vehicles off the roadway. Then use reflectors or flares to guard the scene. The manual names two dangers that this protects everyone present from: leaking fuel and live traffic. So clearing the road keeps the crash from blocking traffic, and the reflectors or flares warn approaching drivers that something is ahead. This is one reason the manual suggests carrying flares in your car. The manual says the guarding is for everybody present, which includes you, the other people involved, and anyone who stops to help.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"If you are passing by","fact_ids":["sec12-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Drive past unless aid is lagging.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07"]},{"text":"Keep your eyes on driving.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07"]},{"text":"Follow officer orders.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"If you come upon a crash that you were not part of, keep driving past, unless help has not yet arrived. As you pass, keep your eyes on your own driving and follow any orders from officers at the scene. So passing drivers do not stop to look, and they do not slow traffic to watch. They stop only when aid is lagging and they can help. Rolling past, eyes on the road and on officer orders, is the manual's whole instruction for uninvolved drivers. The manual's two conditions for stopping are simple: aid is lagging, and you can do so safely while following any officer's orders. Otherwise, roll past.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Moving an injured person","fact_ids":["sec12-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Leave the injured where they are.","fact_ids":["sec12-F08"]},{"text":"Move only for fire or mortal danger.","fact_ids":["sec12-F08"]},{"text":"Brace back and neck; drag head-first.","fact_ids":["sec12-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Injured people should stay where they are, unless there is fire or a danger to life. If a move is forced, keep the back and neck straight. Put your arms beneath the person's torso, with your upper arms cradling the neck, and grip the clothes to drag the victim head-first out of danger. So moving an injured person is a last resort, only for fire or deadly danger, and when it is necessary it is done carefully, keeping the spine straight and pulling head-first. Otherwise, leave the person still and wait for the ambulance or rescue.","fact_ids":["sec12-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Stay put unless threatened","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Ordinary scenes: do not move them.","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-F08"]},{"text":"Fire or mortal threat: move them.","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-F08"]},{"text":"Braced, straight, head-first.","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. In an emergency it is natural to want to move an injured person, to help them sit up or get comfortable. The manual says injured bodies stay untouched through ordinary scenes, yet move under fire or mortal threat, with braced straight spines dragged head-first clear. So the question to ask is whether there is fire or a danger to life. If not, leave the person where they are. If so, move them the way the manual describes. Comfort is not a reason to move someone; only real danger is. Fire or mortal threat is the line between leaving a victim still and moving them.","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Downed wires","fact_ids":["sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Do not approach downed wires.","fact_ids":["sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]},{"text":"Wire on the car: stay inside.","fact_ids":["sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]},{"text":"Wait for rescuers.","fact_ids":["sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Downed wires are a special danger at a crash. Do not approach them. If a wire is touching a vehicle, the people inside should stay in the vehicle until rescuers come. The manual frames this as patience both ways: fallen wires keep rescuers back, while wire-touched cars keep riders inside, until crews arrive. So both the people outside and the people inside wait. Nobody tries to move the wire, and nobody climbs out of a car the wire is touching. The rescuers who come are the ones equipped to deal with it. Wires keep everyone waiting until the crews arrive.","fact_ids":["sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check moving the injured","fact_ids":["sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"An injured person at a scene.","fact_ids":["sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09"]},{"text":"When may you move them?","fact_ids":["sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: at a crash scene, when may you move an injured person? Work it out before reading on. The answer is only when there is fire or a danger to life. Otherwise the person stays where they are. If a move is forced, keep the back and neck straight, put your arms beneath the torso with your upper arms cradling the neck, and drag the person head-first by the clothes. And if downed wires are involved, keep back, and anyone inside a car the wire is touching should stay inside until rescuers come. Fire or deadly danger is the only reason to move someone.","fact_ids":["sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Scene safety in short","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Clear the road; guard with flares.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]},{"text":"Move the injured only for danger.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]},{"text":"Stay away from wires.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, move vehicles off the roadway when you can, and use reflectors or flares to guard the scene against leaking fuel and live traffic. Drivers who are not involved roll past unless aid lags, watching their driving and officer orders. Injured people stay put unless there is fire or mortal danger, and a forced move braces the back and neck straight and drags the victim head-first by the clothes. Do not approach downed wires, and people in a car touched by a wire stay inside until rescuers come. Next we cover reporting the crash.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-R03","sec12-F09","sec12-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec12-u03","module_id":"sec12-m03","objective_ids":["sec12-u03"],"title":{"text":"Reporting a crash","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-R05","sec12-F11"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Some crashes must be reported to the motor-vehicle agency by law.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-R05"]},{"text":"Missing the report brings serious penalties, and the insurer does not file it for you.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-R02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Ben's crash injured another driver, and Ben called his insurance company the same day.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-R02"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Insurer notice never satisfies the law; the motor-vehicle report must be filed within ten days.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-R02"]},"result":{"text":"Ben files the motor-vehicle crash report within ten days as well.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking that telling your insurance company counts as reporting the crash.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02"]},"correction":{"text":"Calling insurers starts claims but never files the law's report, which is still due within ten days.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F11"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Injury always reports; property above the line; ten days, not the insurer.","fact_ids":["sec12-R05","sec12-F11"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"How soon must a required crash report go to the motor-vehicle agency?","fact_ids":["sec12-F11"]},"answer":{"text":"Within ten days.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11"]},"rationale":{"text":"Missing it is a misdemeanor that can suspend or revoke driver and owner credentials.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Reporting the crash","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Which crashes must be reported.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]},{"text":"The deadline, and the insurer.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"This last lesson of the crash chapter covers reporting. The manual says certain crashes must be reported to the motor-vehicle agency on a crash report form, explains which crashes those are, sets a deadline, and describes the penalties for missing it. It also makes a point that surprises many drivers: telling your insurance company does not meet the requirement. We will go through the reporting triggers, compare the injury trigger with the property-damage trigger, then cover the deadline and the insurer rule. The forms are available at motor-vehicle offices, from agents and on the agency website.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Which crashes to report","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Any crash with a death or injury.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-R05"]},{"text":"Property damage over one thousand dollars to one victim.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-R05"]},{"text":"Forms at offices, agents, website.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"A crash must be reported to the motor-vehicle agency if anyone was killed or injured, or if property damage to any single victim is more than one thousand dollars. The report goes on a crash form, which you can get at motor-vehicle offices, from agents, or on the agency website. The manual sums up the two kinds of trigger: deaths and injuries always report, while property damage reports only past one thousand dollars to a single victim. So for an injury, there is no threshold at all, while for property damage, you need to know whether that line was crossed.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Harm versus threshold","fact_ids":["sec12-R05","sec12-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Death or injury: always report.","fact_ids":["sec12-R05","sec12-F10"]},{"text":"Property: only above the threshold.","fact_ids":["sec12-R05","sec12-F10"]},{"text":"For a single victim.","fact_ids":["sec12-R05","sec12-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. People assume all crash reports depend on the amount of damage. The manual separates two kinds of trigger. Deaths and injuries always report, while property reports only past one thousand dollars to a single victim, harm-based versus threshold triggers. So a crash with a minor injury and almost no damage still needs a report, because the injury alone triggers it. A crash with no injury needs a report only if one victim's property damage is above the threshold. Ask first whether anyone was hurt, and only then think about the damage amount.","fact_ids":["sec12-R05","sec12-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The deadline and penalties","fact_ids":["sec12-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"File within ten days.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11"]},{"text":"Missing it is a misdemeanor.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11"]},{"text":"Credentials can be suspended or revoked.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"A required report must be filed with the motor-vehicle agency within ten days. Missing the deadline is a misdemeanor, and it can lead to suspension or revocation of both driver and owner credentials. If the driver was hurt, the filing duty passes to passengers or the owner. And the manual is direct about one more point: insurer notice never satisfies the law. Telling your insurance company about the crash is a separate step. It does not take the place of the motor-vehicle report, which you must still file yourself within the ten days.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"The insurer is not the agency","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Calling the insurer starts a claim.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F11"]},{"text":"It never files the required report.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F11"]},{"text":"The ten-day report is still due.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many drivers believe that once they have called their insurance company, the crash has been reported. The manual says calling insurers starts claims but never files law, since motor-vehicle reports still land within ten days under misdemeanor and credential peril. So you may need to do both: notify your insurer to start a claim, and file the crash report with the motor-vehicle agency to meet the law. Skipping the second because you did the first is exactly the mistake that can cost you your license.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the deadline","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-R02","sec12-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"A crash that must be reported.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-R02","sec12-R05"]},{"text":"How soon must it be filed?","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-R02","sec12-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you were in a crash that injured someone, so it must be reported. How soon must the report go to the motor-vehicle agency? Work it out before reading on. The answer is within ten days.
